proposedTags.name: Outside Event Tie-In
proposedTags.draftDefinition: The product attaches itself to an event it does not run and cannot control, invites the user to commit to a position on that event before it happens, and resolves the commitment when the world resolves the event. What the product supplies is the stake and the wait; the reward attached to the outcome is incidental to the pattern and may be small or absent.
proposedTags.conditions: an external event with a known date the product tracks; a commitment the user records before that date, such as a prediction, a selection, a side taken, or an entry; a deadline set by the external event rather than by the product's own clock; and a resolution the product reports once the event has happened. In the observed implementation the product listed real fixtures, gave "13 hours left to choose who's the winner", let the user play the fixture in-product in the interval, and stated that rewards follow "based on real life match results" (O36). A purchased thirty-day reward calendar was separately pinned to the date of a named final (O98).
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: Challenge covers a bounded objective whose success condition the product itself evaluates; here the condition is settled outside the product by something the user cannot influence, and the boundary belongs to a third party's calendar. Variable Reward Outcome covers a resolution the system performs. Daily Claim Pack and Daily Login Rewards cover intervals the product defines. No entry covers the product borrowing an external event's schedule and suspense.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: the pattern does not need a game or a sport. A bank running a promotion against a tournament, a fitness product built around a race date, a news product on election night, a retail product on a results announcement, and a trading product on a scheduled release would all show it. It is describable without reference to this app.
proposedTags.caveat: Held pending a second instance. Only one product has been observed running it, and within that product no commitment was seen resolving: the duel's settlement rule was read from copy rather than watched operating (O36). Before this can be written as an entry it needs a second observed instance in another app, and at least one commitment seen through to its resolution, so that the boundary against Challenge can be drawn on behavior rather than on framing. If settlement turns out to depend only on the user's own in-product play, the pattern collapses into a bounded objective with a themed deadline.

proposedTags.name: Progressive Reveal
proposedTags.draftDefinition: The product withholds something it already holds and discloses it in pieces rather than at once, so that the user returns or acts again to see more of it. The pattern is the drip: what the product charges for a piece, if anything, is incidental, and a reveal released on a schedule is the clearer case because nothing but the wait moves it.
proposedTags.conditions: a withheld item, result, or content set the product has already determined; a stated or implied scope for what is being withheld, such as a pool size or a number of pieces; a route by which one piece is released, whether a timer, an action, or a payment; and a state that persists between releases so the user can see how much remains. In the observed implementations a mystery player item was narrowed clue by clue from a stated pool of 154 (O39), event theme challenges stated "reveals in five days" (O49), and chapter entries stated "unlocks at week three" and "unlocks at week four" (O63).
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: Loot Box and Variable Reward Outcome classify a resolution that happens at once when a commitment is made; this pattern is the opposite shape, a resolution spread deliberately across time or across actions. Progression Gate classifies a part withheld until a measure the user advances reaches a value; here nothing the user does needs to advance, and in the scheduled form the user cannot advance it at all. Season Content Pass classifies an entitlement over grouped content rather than the pacing of its disclosure.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: it recurs wherever a product holds more than it shows, including staged content calendars, teased features, phased result announcements, and serialized releases. It is describable without reference to this app.
proposedTags.caveat: Held pending a second instance. The paid form and the scheduled form were both seen inside this one product, which is not enough to establish that they are one pattern rather than two, and neither was seen operating: no clue was bought and no scheduled reveal was reached (O39, O63). Before this can be written as an entry it needs a second observed instance in another app, and preferably a scheduled reveal watched through at least two of its releases, so the entry can be built on the drip rather than on the price.

system.tagline: One account-level progression hangs almost everything else off it, releasing the product one named feature at a time while the squad it's all spent developing gets sold back from a dozen directions.
system.overview: FC Mobile's system runs on one measure: XP from nearly every activity advances an account level, and that level is what releases the rest of the product in pieces, leagues and the football center at 4, challenge mode at 5, a lineup slot at 8, the market at 9. Because the level is fed by playing anything at all, the order in which the game opens itself isn't something a player chooses. Everything that progression unlocks acts on one object, the squad, players held and developed as their own items, acquired through packs and drafts that are also where the game's currencies converge. Around all of it run three return cadences, daily, weekly and seasonal, deliberately not aligned, so something is always about to close.
system.loop: The loop is: play a match or any of a dozen other named activities, earn XP that advances the account level, cross a level threshold and have another feature released, use that feature to develop the squad, training and ranking up players by consuming other held players and a purchased material, spend earned or purchased currency on packs and drafts to acquire more players, join or build a league whose collective quests and reward track advance only through combined member activity, and return across three separate cadences, a daily login and task list, a weekly head-to-head leaderboard, and a seasonal Star Pass and league season, each running out on its own schedule.
system.keyInsight: The layers feed each other in one direction more than the other. Play produces XP, which produces levels, which release features, which produce more places to play; play also produces Star Pass credits, league points, event tokens and a dozen other balances, each with its own store. What the record doesn't show is the reverse: the monthly cards pay their daily amounts whether or not the user does anything, the tournament-tied calendar is stated to unlock regardless of login, and the purchase ladders advance only by paying. That asymmetry, paid surfaces that don't need play, sitting next to a progression system built entirely from it, is the structural fact this analysis can support.
system.whatMakesItWork: Nothing about the account level asks a new player to choose an order; playing anything at all decides it for them, since every activity feeds the same number. That single measure is also why the monetization surfaces converge where they do: the squad the level-gated features are all built around is exactly what packs, drafts and the transfer market sell, so the shortest path from any point in the product to a purchase is one tap on a currency the player is already holding.

roles.role: Nearly every activity, matches, missions, drafts, skill games, feeds this one measure, and nothing about it lets the user choose what to buy with it; it exists purely to advance the account level.
The account level is a bare number with no name attached, advanced by experience points and announced at each crossing; it's what every other release in the product actually reads.

Reads the account level to release the market, leagues, challenge mode, the scouting camp, a lineup slot and club challenge, one at a time, in an order the player never chooses since every activity feeds the same measure.

The squad is what all of that progression acts on: players held separately from the account, developed by consuming other held players and a purchased material, and assigned to a limited number of active positions.
Drafts and packs are how the squad is actually acquired, resolving to a stated player pool with published pity rules on some offers and none at all on others.

Money enters as FC points and silver, and both are spent on the same packs and drafts that acquire the squad, with every currency display in the top bar doubling as a route into the store that sells it.
Coins, gems and a set of campaign-specific tokens are earned through ordinary play and spent on the same packs, drafts and squad-development costs the paid currencies also buy.
Three locked sequences advance only by paying, isolated entirely from play; the one named a streak has no continuity condition in it at all, just ten packs bought strictly in order.
Leagues hold their own season level, point total and hundred-position reward track, advanced only by members' combined activity; an inactive roster stalls the whole structure at once.
Leagues are ranked twice over, on a group board with promotion and relegation and on a worldwide board, while a separate weekly board ranks head-to-head players by wins.

The Star Pass runs roughly sixty positions advanced by credits earned in the same activities that feed experience points, resetting on a stated season boundary the product announces without ever explaining what it costs the player.
Two separate login calendars run in parallel on their own schedules, each paying for the act of opening the app on a new day and for nothing else.

connections.title: Every activity feeds one number
connections.desc: XP from matches, missions, drafts and skill games all advance the same account level, with nothing else in the interface treating that level as worth naming.
connections.effect: The level becomes the product's real spine without ever being presented as one: a bare number crossed as a side effect of doing almost anything.

connections.title: The level is what the gates read
connections.desc: The market, leagues, the football center, challenge mode, the scouting camp, a lineup slot and club challenge are all released at stated account levels.
connections.effect: A single number decides the order in which the whole product opens itself to a new player, and that order isn't something the player is choosing.

connections.title: Gated features are gated squad routes
connections.desc: The market unlocks at level 9 and a lineup slot at level 8, both of them routes specifically for acquiring or fielding more players.
connections.effect: The pacing of squad growth is set by the same level that paces everything else, rather than by anything the player decides about their own team.

connections.title: Packs and drafts are how the squad grows
connections.desc: Player items are acquired through packs and drafts that resolve to one of a stated pool, several publishing exact odds and some publishing none at all.
connections.effect: Building the squad and gambling on a pack's contents are, in this product, the same action.

connections.title: The undisclosed pool is priced in real money
connections.desc: Store packs commit FC points or silver before their contents resolve, with FC points sold directly for money across seven price points.
connections.effect: The clearest route from a real purchase to an unknown result runs straight through the currency the game sells for cash.

connections.title: Developing a player spends earned balances
connections.desc: Training consumes other held players, and ranking up consumes rank-up points sold and earned through ordinary play.
connections.effect: The squad isn't just what currency buys, it's also what currency is spent developing, tying earned balances to squad growth at every stage.

connections.title: The ladders are paid for, never played for
connections.desc: All three purchase sequences, including the one named a streak, advance strictly by buying the position beneath the next one, with no activity route into any of them.
connections.effect: This is the one part of the monetization system with no connection back to play at all: money is the only input, in a fixed order.

connections.title: The pass runs the same shape as the level
connections.desc: Star Pass credits are earned from the same Division Rivals and live-event play that feeds account XP, accumulating toward roughly sixty positions and resetting at the season boundary.
connections.effect: A player advancing their account level is, without any separate decision, also advancing the pass.

connections.title: Standing runs above and inside the league
connections.desc: Leagues are ranked against each other on a group board with promotion and relegation and on a worldwide board, while members are separately ranked by contribution inside their own league.
connections.effect: A league's collective activity produces two independent kinds of standing at once, one competing outward and one measuring each member against their own teammates.
